Foreign policy during and after the 1971 crisis

India's foreign policy during the 1971 Bangladesh crisis demonstrated how a country could combine non-alignment with practical diplomatic cooperation.

India faced a complex international situation involving Pakistan, China, the USA and the USSR. Its decisions reflected both the principle of independent foreign-policy judgment and the need to protect national security.

The India-USSR Treaty of 1971

India and the Soviet Union signed the Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation on 9 August 1971.

The treaty was signed in New Delhi by Indian External Affairs Minister Swaran Singh and Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko.

The treaty provided for political cooperation and consultation in the event of an attack or threat against either country.

Article IV expressly recognised India's policy of non-alignment. Article IX provided for immediate consultations and appropriate measures in the event of an attack or threat. It did not establish an automatic obligation for one country to enter a war on behalf of the other.

The treaty was concluded for an initial period of 20 years.

Nevertheless, India's close relationship with the Soviet Union generated debate over whether Indian foreign policy had developed a pro-Soviet orientation.

India's 1971 treaty with the USSR was a major strategic partnership, but it was not equivalent to India's formal membership of the Warsaw Pact.

The Simla Agreement of 1972

After the 1971 war, India and Pakistan negotiated a political settlement.

The Simla Agreement was signed by Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and Pakistani leader Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.

The official agreement is dated 2 July 1972 and entered into force on 4 August 1972.

The agreement established important principles for relations between the 2 countries:

  • Disputes should be settled through bilateral negotiations or other peaceful means mutually agreed upon.
  • Both countries should respect each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
  • Neither country should seek to alter the situation unilaterally while disputes remain unresolved.
  • Both countries should respect the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir resulting from the December 1971 ceasefire, without prejudice to their respective positions.

The agreement sought to restore peaceful relations, but it did not settle every outstanding dispute.

Three important diplomatic agreements

India-USSR Treaty9 August 1971Peace, friendship, cooperation and security consultations

The end of the Cold War in 1991

The Soviet Union disintegrated in December 1991. Its disintegration brought an end to the Cold War's established bipolar international order.

During the Cold War, non-alignment had primarily meant avoiding membership of the 2 rival superpower-led military blocs. With the disappearance of one superpower and the end of that rivalry, this particular purpose became less important.

However, the underlying objective of independent foreign-policy decision-making remained relevant.

From Cold War non-alignment to broader strategic autonomy

India adapted to the changed international environment by seeking wider relations with major powers and other partners.

The changing global context placed greater emphasis on economic cooperation, access to technology, trade, investment and national security.

The central distinction is between a Cold War policy and a continuing national objective:

  • Cold War non-alignment: Avoiding membership of military blocs led by the USA and USSR.
  • Continuing strategic autonomy: Maintaining the freedom to decide foreign-policy matters according to national interests, even while cooperating with multiple international partners.

Strategic autonomy therefore does not require identical relations with every country. India may cooperate more closely with one country on defence, another on trade and several countries on international development without necessarily accepting a permanent commitment to follow any one of them on every issue.

Continuing relevance of NAM

The Non-Aligned Movement did not disappear with the Soviet Union. Its activities continued to address international peace, development, economic inequalities and the concerns of developing countries.

Its historical objectives of decolonisation and freedom from Cold War bloc pressure were supplemented by wider concerns regarding international economic cooperation and representation.

As of the 22 November 2026 content cutoff, the official NAM website identifies Uganda's chairmanship as covering 2024-2027. The 19th NAM Summit took place in Kampala, Uganda, in January 2024. These are the verified summit and chairmanship details for that period, not permanent institutional facts.

NAM remains a distinct international movement, while strategic autonomy is a foreign-policy objective that a country can pursue independently of any particular movement.

Overall significance

India's post-independence foreign policy developed through changing circumstances. Non-alignment helped preserve diplomatic independence during the Cold War. Panchsheel expressed principles of peaceful coexistence, while the wars of 1962, 1965 and 1971 highlighted the importance of national security and territorial integrity.

After 1991, India's international relations increasingly reflected cooperation with multiple partners in a world no longer divided into the same 2 superpower-led blocs.

The connecting idea throughout these phases is that foreign policy must balance national independence, security, peaceful relations and development.

Prelims focus

  • India-USSR Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation: 9 August 1971.
  • The 1971 treaty expressly recognised India's non-alignment in Article IV.
  • Simla Agreement: 2 July 1972, according to the official agreement text.
  • The Soviet Union disintegrated in December 1991.
  • Strategic autonomy remained relevant after the Cold War.
  • The 19th NAM Summit was held in Kampala, Uganda, in January 2024.
  • Trap: The end of the Cold War did not mean the dissolution of NAM or the end of India's pursuit of independent foreign-policy choices.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, chapters 1-2, printed pp. 10-13 and 17-20; NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, printed pp. 76-79; Ministry of External Affairs, Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation between India and the USSR, 9 August 1971, Articles IV, IX and XI; Ministry of External Affairs, Simla Agreement, 2 July 1972, clauses 1-4; Non-Aligned Movement, official Uganda Chairmanship website, History and Summit information, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: An unbroken line links India's early Cold War choices and wars to wider partnerships after 1991 and the 2024 NAM Summit.
pictures.caption: India's continuing objective is independent decision-making, although the international conditions have changed.

title: Foreign-Policy Treaties and the Changing Global Context After 1971
